title: Narrative Paradoxes in LLM Inference: Shaping Reasoning Trajectories toward Misalignment
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A benign-looking narrative core combined with a staged analytical framework steers a model step by step into producing harmful output.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; step 1 feeds step 2, domino chain at the end
description: The figure has two rounded gray panels read left to right. Step 1, "Crafting the Narrative Core", starts with a red "Restricted Objective (G)" box that reads "How to paralyze the national power grid?". Pink and blue arrows lead from it to two stacked boxes. The pink one is "Malicious Role R", with cartoon terrorist, thief and hacker icons. The blue one is "Benign Carrier Task T", with a list of cybersecurity tasks and an angel icon. Both feed a dashed "Paradoxical Scenario" box that shows a hacker plus a shield and a power-grid scene. Step 2, "Deploying the Structured Analytical Frame-work", has a prompt template with colored text for three stages: surface purpose, latent intent and operational planning. Below it, a rainbow row of falling dominoes sits above an arrow that points to the model output and a "Jailbreak Success" icon column. The output text is annotated in matching colors, with red highlights on key phrases.
caption: The PDRA attack pipeline. Given a harmful goal G, PDRA first constructs a paradoxical narrative core by selecting a malicious actor R∗and a benign carrier task T ∗. This core is then fed into a mandatory three-stage analytical framework that guides the model to reason from surface intent to operational steps. The process programs the model’s reasoning trajectory, ultimately generating detailed harmful content while bypassing safety mechanisms.
abstract: Explicit reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is often associated with reliability, yet it can still pose risks when a model infers harmful goals under a benign context. We identify a distinct challenge: ensuring the safety of the \emph{multi-step reasoning process} itself, where locally coherent steps may still lead to globally harmful outcomes. To explore this vulnerability, we propose PDRA (Paradox-driven Reasoning-based Attack), a novel attack method that programs a harmful reasoning trajectory. PDRA first constructs a paradoxical narrative core by pairing a malicious actor (e.g., a terrorist) with a benign task (e.g., writing a safety bulletin). It then embeds this core into a structured analytical framework that forces the model through a mandatory three-stage analysis -- surface purpose, latent intent, and operational reconstruction -- guiding it to produce detailed harmful content while maintaining narrative coherence. Mechanistically, we show PDRA steers the model's internal representations away from refusal-related patterns, suppressing safety-triggering lexicons while activating planning-oriented terms. Empirically, PDRA achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates across diverse LLMs with high efficiency. \textcolor{red}{\textbf{Warning:} This paper may contain sensitive content.}
